draft.title: Vertices, edges and degree
card: a point on a graph, often drawn as a dot. It can stand for a place, a person or a team.
a line that joins two vertices. It can stand for a road, a friendship or a match between two teams.
the number of edges that meet a vertex. A vertex with 3 edges meeting it has degree 3.
Example: a graph has vertices A, B, C and D, with edges AB, AC, AD and BC. A has 3 edges meeting it, so its degree is 3. D has only AD, so its degree is 1.
draft.remember: Count the edges at a vertex to find its degree, not the vertices it touches by name.

a.q: A graph has vertices P, Q, R and S, and edges PQ, PR, PS and QR. What is the degree of vertex R?
a.why: The edges meeting R are PR and QR, so the degree of R is 2. The answer 3 is the degree of P, which has PQ, PR and PS.
a.clue: List only the edges that include the letter R.

b.q: A graph shows five towns as vertices and has 6 edges for the roads between them. The towns have degrees 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2. Which town has the most roads meeting it?
b.why: Degree is the number of edges meeting a vertex, so the largest degree has the most roads. The largest degree listed is 3. The number 6 counts all the edges on the graph, not the edges at one town.
b.clue: Which degree in the list is the largest?

problems.detail: The contrast 'not the vertices it touches by name' is unclear. In a simple graph like the card's example, counting edges and counting neighbouring vertices give the same number, so students may not see what mistake they are being warned about.
The stem lists the degrees, so a student only has to pick the largest number. The clue says exactly that, so the question barely tests the idea of degree at Year 11 level.

proposal.title: Vertices, edges and degree
card: a point on a graph, often drawn as a dot. It can stand for a place, a person or a team.
a line that joins two vertices. It can stand for a road, a friendship or a match between two teams.
the number of edges that meet a vertex. Each edge joins two vertices, so it adds 1 to the degree of both of them.
Example: a graph has edges AB, AC, AD and BC. A meets AB, AC and AD, so its degree is 3. B meets AB and BC, so its degree is 2, even though B is named second in AB.
proposal.remember: Degree counts the edges at one vertex. Check every edge, whichever end the vertex is named at.

a.q: A graph has vertices P, Q, R and S, and edges PQ, PR, PS and QR. What is the degree of vertex R?
a.why: The edges meeting R are PR and QR, so the degree of R is 2. The answer 3 is the degree of P, which has PQ, PR and PS.
a.clue: List only the edges that include the letter R.

b.q: A graph shows roads between towns: Ash–Bell, Ash–Cole, Ash–Dale, Bell–Cole, Cole–Dale and Cole–Eden. Which town has the largest degree?
b.why: Cole meets Ash–Cole, Bell–Cole, Cole–Dale and Cole–Eden, so its degree is 4, more than Ash's 3. Counting only roads where a town is named first makes Ash look largest, but an edge counts at both ends. The number 6 is the total number of roads, not the roads at one town.
b.clue: A town can be named second in a road and still meet it.
